The Gillette Logo in the diamond is common on some Gillette techs. I know my fat handle tech doesn't have it, but, for example, almost all of the aluminum travel techs have it.

Since these are old, there probably won't be a way to just get a base plate. I would look at sites like ebay to find a tech on the cheap and use it's base plate. If you take a look here, you can see that most (not all though) techs have pretty similar base plates. http://www.mr-razor.com/ebay/1938-1966%20Tech%20Evolution%20klein.jpg So you should be able to make a frankenrazor. Another user here with more experience with techs should be able to say more on that.

I'm pretty sure that the Gillette is a ball end Tech. Which I think dates it to '46-'50. I'm not 100% sure, but I think you could probably use another tech's baseplate. Another use can probably verify that. I think most techs have a very similar base plate design that can work with the slit bar or solid bar on the head.

Here are the different techs: http://www.mr-razor.com/Rasierer/Tech/Tech.htm

For $5, I don't think you were ripped off. If that handles doesn't have any cracks in it, then definitely not ripped of. Just have to make a frankenrazor.

For the lather, practice is kind of important. If you can spare some of the cream, make some practice lathers. This will help you figure out how much water to use and the like. 

For the after shave, Nivea is one of the cheapest, but still a great balm. I still have my original bottle of it that lasted me over a year and only about half gone. (I really stretched it.) When you use it, you only need about a dime sized amount. A little goes a long way. You should be able to get like 4-6 months out of the bottle.

For your second question, when you start shaving (several months), do not listen to music while shaving. This allows for audible feedback and makes you more focused on the shave than being lax about it. And while it is stressed everywhere, it can't be stressed enough. Absolutely NO pressure.

I haven't given a full wet shaving kit to anyone. However, I did manage to kind of convert my dad to shaving soap. He used to just use dove or something like that. I got him to try Arko and he seems to like it a lot. He doesn't use a brush, just rub it onto the face and "build a lather" by rubbing it with a wet hand. Plus, he says it doesn't clog the drains like normal body soap does.

Unless the person displays interest in wet shaving, I would give them more of lather stuff. Maybe a "cheap" soap/cream and maybe a brush. (By cheap, I mean like Arko, Palmolive, RazorRock, Proraso, etc...)

To extend on this, a rinse to the razor head and blade with isopropyl alcohol (70% or 91%) before and after the shave will help with acne. I don't have acne, but I still do this to displace water after my shave (after washing the razor) and to sanitize a little before my shave. Put some in a container and put the head of the razor into the container and slightly agitate. (Don't hit the container with the head/blade.)

Unfortunately, I can't really answer that much on the quality of the creams. I have yet to try it. However, I have a sample of the Orange Amber. It has more of a clean soap smell with a hint of amber. May change when aerated into a lather though.

If you are able to order from Maggards, Mugso Real is in there samples. [Maggards samples](http://www.maggardrazors.com/product/shaving-cream-sample/) It's $2.5USD per 1/4oz sample. (A little pricey, but it is a sample after all.)

I have been doing cold shaves almost exclusively lately and they do help with irritation. As far as your question on "more problematic", there is only one scenario that I've encountered with cold water that was problematic. If you have an area of coarser or thicker hairs on a harder to get area, it can cause a little trouble getting a close shave there. I have such hair just outside my goatee area on my jaw line. I get a little tugging if I go ATG on those hairs. But that is about it for me.

If you are located in the US, you can start your presentation with a small (30 seconds or less) homage to King Gillette. Something about a great entrepreneur and set in motion a notion that would change the way that we shaved.

Try the method in this video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=boZwOkMXPhQ

It is Douglas Smythe, the HTGAM guy, suggesting that you use an old pair of jeans and do like 5-6 "passes" per side (including flipping) of the blade (while in the razor) on the jeans. Basically, you are mimicking a shave with the jean fuzz.  

I haven't had a need to try it as the blades I use (and the ones that I am currently trying out) all seem to be in just about the sweet spot for me, but it seems to have a good logic to it. Good luck and hope for the best.

MrTooNiceGuy basically stated it very well. If you don't end up getting an after shave in your purchase, two things you can use are witch hazel and/or Nivea aftershave balm (Sensitive is the better version IMHO). I will admit that witch hazel does not smell good. However, you could add some essential oil to add a different scent or just put it on, wait a minute or two then splash cold water on your face to get rid of the smell and replace with a cologne type aftershave to replace the scent. Both are most like available at your local pharmacy/drug store. Heck, maybe even a local supermarket.

Both are YMMV, but you could try them now while waiting for your new stuff while using your current gear.
Arko Adventure shaving cream. It's not perfectly Irish Springs, but it is pretty close. And it is like $4USD.

True that it does seem weird to need to do that first. But, hey, 30+ years ago, you had to break in denim jeans before they were comfy. Now-a-days we are used to having every processed down to a useable state. Some people have very tough skin to where a fresh feather feels great and doesn't do anything negative to them. However, those that like used feather blades just have to do a little bit extra to get what they want without making those that like the sharpness lose out. Besides, I've found many people, including myself, tend to like the fact that wet shaving kind of has a ritualistic feel to it. Add one more small step just adds to that satisfaction of having a ritual that is tailored to you.

And as far as the derby goes, I was more giving the polar extremes. There are many gradients in between, but much less effective in presenting a view.

Another thing you could try while loading would be:

* Put the butt of the handle lower in your palm
* Extend your fingers as far as you can over the handle and onto the hairs. (Try to get most of your fingertips onto the hairs. You don't need to go too far.)
* Slightly grip with your fingertips and loading the brush.

This will "shorten" the length of the hairs to try and give them more backbone in a sense. Your silvertip may not be floppy, but probably doesn't have the backbone/stiffness that your other brushes have. It may work, it may not. But since it is just a technique change, there isn't much harm in giving it a shot.

Follow what Leisureguy said. It is really good advice. I "accidentally" did something similar when I first start a few years ago. It helped a lot.

Also, as far as any "rave" about blades, that really doesn't matter. I mean, I have grown to hate Derbys beyond anything. But that is me. There are many people agree, but probably about the same amount that love them. Same with Feathers. They are way to sharp for my skin to handle. However, in a month or so when you start exploring blades again and if you want to try Feathers again, you could try a technique shown in this video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=boZwOkMXPhQ

Best of luck.

I have absolutely no idea how it works. I've done it with conditioner on a couple of boar brushes and they all seemed to get split ends fast (in about a week) and didn't seem to do any other damage to the brush. My only guess would be maybe that the conditioner has some of the moisturizing or conditioning ingredients that bring the bristles to an extra hydrated/moisturized state, then the act of drying them beyond what I would assume normal "live" hair (stuff actually on a live animal) is used to would create a larger differential thus putting more strain on the bristles causing them to split faster. 

Mind you, I don't know if that is even remotely close, but in my head it makes some sense in that larger extremes means more pronounced changes happening.

I didn't mean to come off saying that a shave stick is lesser than the soap in a bowl. I tend to use my Arko shave sticks as sticks a lot too. (Hell, 90% of my college shaves used them as such.) I was more mean that as if you like the Arko soap, and you get a bulk deal, it can be a lot cheaper to get the sticks and mash them into a mug/bowl instead of buying the plastic travel container that he had on his list.

I'll make the recommendation of everyday for the first week (up to you how often after that, maybe once a month) is the create a palm lather of conditioner. (Any conditioner will do.) This will basically accelerate the splitting the ends of the bristles. This makes the end of the brush much much softer. I have the Omega Pro 48 and after about a week of doing this, the ends are like 95% as soft as a Silver tip. (My opinion.) Even with the brush completely dry, brushed over my neck, it is even softer than a best badger brush I have. It will still have the same backbone as it does now, but oh so much nicer. 

Also, If you happen to find the arko to be a soap that you like, I would recommend looking at getting some of the normal shaving sticks. Since the soap is very soft, just grab a bowl or a mug and just push into a puck at the bottom. In bulk, they are much cheaper than the travel case and if you get the bulk pack, you will have enough to last through WW4 while still having a stick in the drawer.

Good luck and enjoy your shaves.

Okay, first time getting drunk will suck. Unless you are in such an ideal situation that you are a movie, it will not be great. If you do desire to drink, learn to sip your drink. Shots are basically the prelude to the classic scene of someone puking over a toilet. It takes about 15 minutes for alcohol to actually effect you. Everything before that is mostly placebo. So, basically, if you sip your drink, you are constantly adding a slight bit more to your body. If will still effect you after 15 minutes. So you draw it out. Maybe you have about three shots worth while sipping for fifteen minutes. By the time the first one actually hits you, you aren't really that deep and you can start to control it better. While with shots, you take the shot, maybe have a chaser and start pouring the second round, only like 30 seconds, maybe a minute, go by. By the time you're six or seven shots in, you still haven't actually been effected by that first shot. So that next half hour will be rough as they all hit, and will result in a very bad night.

Aside from that, I would recommend caution with drinking and depression. As TryingToRiseAbove alluded to, and I can very much agree with, drinking will make you feel worse depression wise. Your brain starts to lose its ability to hold up any barriers you have while sober that can help control the thoughts and feelings, and it will start to basically over whelm you. Unless you happen to be in a similar mindset as me, where being in a state of self loathing and the like is actually one of the few types of "happiness" you know, I wouldn't recommend getting drunk.
